en: Vibhaṅga:
Analysis of the Elements 1.
The Exposition According to the Discourses (Suttantabhājanīya)
Six elements:
the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, and the consciousness element.
Therein, what is the earth element?
The earth element is twofold:
there is the internal, and there is the external.
Therein, what is the internal earth element?
Whatever internally, within oneself, is hard, solid, hardness, the state of being hard, the quality of being hard, and is clung to (*upādinnam*), namely:
head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, gorge, feces; or whatever else there is...
Whatever internally, in oneself, is hard, harshness, the state of being hard, the quality of hardness, and is clung-to internally—
this is called the internal earth element.
Therein, what is the external earth element?
Whatever is external, hard, harsh, hardness, the state of being hard, not clung to externally, namely:
iron, copper, tin, lead, brass, pearl, gem, beryl, conch shell, stone, coral, silver, gold, ruby, cat's-eye, grass, wood, gravel, potsherd, earth, rock, and mountain. Whatever...
Or whatever else there is externally that is hard, harsh, hardness, the state of being hard, external and not clung-to—
this is called the "external earth element.
Whatever is the internal earth element and whatever is the external earth element, having gathered these together and condensed them into one—
This is called the earth element.
In this context, what is the water element? There are two kinds of water element:
There is the internal and there is the external.
Therein, what is the internal water element?
That which is internal, belonging to oneself, liquid, of the nature of liquid, viscous, of the nature of viscosity, the state of cohesion of form, internal and clung-to (appropriated), namely:
Bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, synovial fluid, urine,
or whatever else there is internally, belonging to oneself, that is liquid, of a liquid nature, viscous, of a viscous nature, the cohesion of matter,
internal and clung-to.
This is called the internal water element.
In this context, what is the external water element?
That which is external, belonging to water, of the nature of water, moisture, of the nature of moisture, the state of cohesion of matter, not clung to internally; namely:
Root-juice, stem-juice, bark-juice, leaf-juice, flower-juice, fruit-juice, milk, curd, ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses,
or waters from the earth or from the sky; or whatever else there is externally that is water,
watery, viscous, viscid, and bound up with external form, not clung to [by craving and views].
This is called the "external water element.
Whatever is the internal water element and whatever is the external water element, having gathered these together and condensed them into one—
this is called the "water element."
In this context, what is the fire element?
The fire element is twofold:
there is the internal and there is the external.
In this context, what is the internal fire element?
Whatever is internal, belonging to oneself, that is fire, of the nature of fire, heat, of the nature of heat, warmth, of the nature of warmth, and is clung to internally;
namely, that by which one is warmed, by which one ages, by which one is consumed, and that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted [is digested].
Whatever else there is internally, belonging to oneself, that is fire, of the nature of fire, heat,
of the nature of heat, warmth, of the nature of warmth, and is clung-to internally—
this is called the internal fire element.
In this context, what is the external fire element?
That which is external, belonging to fire, heat, belonging to heat, warmth, belonging to warmth, not clung to internally; namely:
a wood-fire, a chaff-fire, a grass-fire, a cow-dung-fire, a husk-fire, a refuse-fire, a forest-fire, the heat of a fire, the heat of the sun, and so forth.
The heat of a heap of wood, the heat of a heap of grass, the heat of a heap of grain, the heat of a heap of goods;
or whatever else there is that is external fire, fiery, heat, heated, warmth, warmed, and not clung to externally—
this is called the "external fire element."
Whatever internal fire element there is, and whatever external fire element there is— having gathered these together and condensed them into one—
this is called the "fire element.
In this context, what is the air element?
The wind element is twofold:
there is the internal, and there is the external.
In this regard, what is the internal wind element?
Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is air or airy, a state of distension, and is clung-to internally as form; that is to say:

upward-moving winds, downward-moving winds, winds in the belly, winds in the bowels, winds coursing through the limbs and members, piercing winds, razor-like winds, lotus-stalk-like winds, or in-breath and out-breath—or whatever else there is.
Whatever internally, within oneself, is air or airy, a state of distension, and is clung-to internally as matter—
this is called the internal air element.
In this context, what is the external air element?
Whatever external air there is, or that which has become air, the state of rigidity of matter, not clung to externally, namely: eastern winds,
western winds, northern winds, southern winds, dusty winds, dustless winds,
cold winds, hot winds, limited winds, excessive winds, black winds, *verambha* winds, winged winds, and garuḍa winds.
The wind from a fan, the wind from a whisk, or whatever else there is externally that is air, airy, and rigid—
a state of matter that is external and not clung to—
this is called the "external air element."
Whatever internal air element there is, and whatever external air element there is— having gathered these together and condensed them into one—
this is called the "air element.
In this context, what is the space element?
The space element is twofold:
there is the internal and there is the external.
Therein, what is the internal space element?
Whatever internally, within oneself, is space or spatial, void or void-like, an opening or open-like, not in contact with flesh and blood, and is clung-to internally; that is to say:

the ear-cavities, the nose-cavities, the mouth-opening, that by which one swallows what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, where what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted remains, and that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted passes out from the lower part...
Whatever else there is internally, within oneself, that is space, belonging to space, an opening, belonging to an opening,
a cavity, belonging to a cavity, not touched by flesh and blood, and internally clung-to—
this is called the internal space element.
In this context, what is the external space element?
That which is external, space, belonging to space, an opening, belonging to an opening, a cavity, belonging to a cavity, not in contact with the four great elements, and not clung to externally—
this is called the "external space element."
Whatever internal space-element and whatever external space-element there are, having gathered them together and condensed them into one—
this is called the "space-element.
In this context, what is the consciousness-element?
The eye-consciousness element, the ear-consciousness element, the nose-consciousness element, the tongue-consciousness element, the body-consciousness element, and the mind-consciousness element—
this is called the "consciousness element.
These are the six elements.
There are also six elements:
the element of pleasure, the element of pain, the element of mental joy, the element of mental grief, the element of equanimity, and the element of ignorance.
In this context, what is the element of pleasure?
That which is bodily ease, bodily pleasure, the pleasant and pleasurable feeling born of body-contact, the pleasant and pleasurable sensation born of body-contact—
this is called the "pleasure element" (sukhadhātu).
In this context, what is the "pain element" (dukkhadhātu)?
That which is bodily displeasure, bodily suffering, the unpleasant and painful feeling born of body-contact, the unpleasant and painful sensation born of body-contact—
this is called the "element of suffering" (dukkhadhātu).
In this context, what is the element of mental joy (somanassadhātu)?
That mental state which is agreeable, that mental state which is pleasant, the agreeable and pleasant feeling born of mental contact, the agreeable and pleasant sensation born of mental contact—
this is called the element of joy (*somanassadhātu*).
In this context, what is the element of grief (*domanassadhātu*)?
That which is mental unease, mental suffering, the unpleasant and painful feeling born of mental contact, the unpleasant and painful sensation born of mental contact—
this is called the element of grief (*domanassadhātu*).
In this context, what is the element of equanimity (*upekkhādhātu*)?

That mental state which is neither pleasant nor unpleasant, born of mind-contact, an experience that is neither painful nor pleasant, a feeling born of mind-contact that is neither painful nor pleasant—
this is called the "element of equanimity" (*upekkhādhātu*).
In this context, what is the "element of ignorance" (*avijjādhātu*)?
That which is ignorance, non-seeing, non-comprehension, non-awakening, non-enlightenment, non-penetration, lack of grasping, lack of thorough investigation, lack of observation, lack of reflection,
lack of direct realization, dullness, folly, lack of clear comprehension, delusion, extreme delusion, total delusion, ignorance,

the flood of ignorance, the yoke of ignorance, the underlying tendency to ignorance, the obsession of ignorance, the snare of ignorance, and the root of unwholesomeness that is delusion— this is called ignorance.
This is called the "element of ignorance.
These are the six elements.
There are another six elements:
The element of sensual desire, the element of ill will, the element of cruelty, the element of renunciation, the element of non-ill will, and the element of non-cruelty.
Therein, what is the element of sensual desire?
It is reasoning, thought, intention, absorption, application, mental engagement, and wrong intention associated with sensual desire.
This is called the sense-sphere element (kāmadhātu).
Bounded below by the Avīci hell and bounded above by the Paranimmitavasavatti devas,
whatever is included within this interval— namely, the aggregates, elements, and bases, as well as forms and feelings that have their range and inclusion therein— is the sense-sphere element.
Perception, volitional formations, and consciousness—
this is called the "sense-sphere element" (kāmadhātu).
In this context, what is the "element of ill will" (byāpādadhātu)?
Thought and applied thought associated with ill will, up to and including wrong intention—
this is called the "element of ill will.
Or, it is the resentment, hostility, resistance, opposition, anger, and intense anger of the mind toward the ten grounds for resentment.
Provocation, malice, resentment, ill-will, hostility of mind, mental corruption, anger, being angry, the state of being angry,
hatred, hating, the state of hating, hostility, antagonism, opposition, confrontation,
ferocity, abruptness, and displeasure of mind.
This is called the “element of ill will.
In that regard, what is the element of cruelty?
It is the cogitation, initial application of thought, and so forth, associated with cruelty, up to wrong intention.
This is called the "element of cruelty.

Here, someone harms beings with the hand, or with a clod, or with a staff, or with a sword, or with a rope, or with one or another [weapon]; whatever such harming, injuring, hurting, cruelty, vexing, provoking, or assault there is—this is called the "element of cruelty."
In this context, what is the element of renunciation?
Thought and applied thought associated with renunciation …pe… right intention—
this is called the "element of renunciation."
All wholesome states are the "element of renunciation.
In this context, what is the "element of non-ill will"?
It is thought, applied thought, and so forth, associated with non-ill will, up to right intention.
This is called the "element of non-ill will.
That which is loving-kindness toward beings, the state of loving-kindness, the act of loving-kindness, and liberation of mind through loving-kindness—
this is called the "element of non-ill will."
In this context, what is the element of non-harming?
Reasoning, initial application, intention, absorption, sustained application, mental directedness, and right intention associated with non-harming—
this is called the "element of non-harming."
That which is compassion toward sentient beings, the state of being compassionate, the quality of being compassionate, and the liberation of mind through compassion—
this is called the "element of non-violence.
These are the six elements.
Thus, having gathered these three sets of six together and condensed them, they constitute the eighteen elements.
This concludes the Suttanta-bhājaniya. 2.
The Abhidhamma-bhājaniya.
The eighteen elements:
the eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, the ear-consciousness element;
the nose element, the odor element, the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element.
The body element, the tangible-object element, the body-consciousness element, the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.
Therein, what is the eye element?
That eye which, derived from the four great elements, is sensitivity ... [as before] ... this is an empty village.
This is called the "eye-element.
In this context, what is the "form-element"?
That form which, derived from the four great elements, is color and luster … [as before] … this is the form-element.
This is called the "form element" (rūpadhātu).
In this context, what is the eye-consciousness element (cakkhuviññāṇadhātu)?

It is the consciousness, the mind, the mentation, the heart, the lucidity, the mind, the mind-base, the mind-faculty, the consciousness, the aggregate of consciousness, and the corresponding eye-consciousness element that arises dependent upon the eye and forms.
This is called the "eye-consciousness element.
Therein, what is the ear element?
That which is the ear, derived from the four great elements, a sensitivity... [as before] ...this village is empty.
This is called the "ear element.
In this context, what is the sound element?
That sound which, derived from the four great elements, is invisible and impinging... [as before] ...this is the sound element.
This is called the sound element (*saddhadhātu*).
In this context, what is the ear-consciousness element (*sotaviññāṇadhātu*)?

It is the consciousness, mind, mentation, heart, purity, mind, mind-base, mind-faculty, consciousness, aggregate of consciousness, and the corresponding ear-consciousness element that arises dependent upon the ear and sounds.
This is called the ear-consciousness element (*sotaviññāṇadhātu*).
Therein, what is the nose element (*ghānadhātu*)?
That nose which, derived from the four great elements, is sensitivity … [as before] … this is an empty village.
This is called the nose element (*ghānadhātu*).
In this context, what is the odor element (*gandhadhātu*)?
That odor which, derived from the four great elements, is invisible and impinging … [as before] … this is the odor element.
This is called the "odor element.
In this context, what is the nose-consciousness element?

It is the consciousness, mind, mentation, heart, clarity, mind, mind-base, mind-faculty, consciousness, aggregate of consciousness, and the corresponding nose-consciousness element that arises dependent upon the nose and odors.
This is called the nose-consciousness element.
Therein, what is the tongue element?
That which is the sensitivity derived from the four great elements … [as before] … this is an empty village.
This is called the tongue element (*jivhādhātu*).
In this context, what is the taste element (*rasadhātu*)?
That taste which, derived from the four great elements, is invisible and impinging … [as before] … this is the taste element.
This is called the “taste element.
In this context, what is the tongue-consciousness element?

Depending upon the tongue and tastes, there arises consciousness, mind, mentation, heart, clarity, the mind, the mind-base, the mind-faculty, consciousness, the aggregate of consciousness, and the corresponding tongue-consciousness element.
This is called the tongue-consciousness element (*jivhāviññāṇadhātu*).
In this context, what is the body element (*kāyadhātu*)?
That which is the sensitive matter derived from the four great elements belonging to the body … [as before] … this is an empty village.
This is called the "body element" (kāyadhātu).
Therein, what is the "tangible object element" (phoṭṭhabbadhātu)?
The earth element... [and so forth] ...this is the tangible object element.
This is called the "tangible element" (*phoṭṭhabbadhātu*).
In this context, what is the "body-consciousness element" (*kāyaviññāṇadhātu*)?

It is that consciousness, mind, mentation, heart, purity, mind, mind-base, mind-faculty, consciousness, the aggregate of consciousness, and the corresponding body-consciousness element that arises dependent upon the body and tangible objects.
This is called the "body-consciousness element.
In this context, what is the mind element (*manodhātu*)?

It is that consciousness, mind, mentality, heart, clarity, mind, mind-base, mind-faculty, consciousness, the aggregate of consciousness, and the corresponding mind element, which arises immediately after the eye-consciousness element has arisen and ceased.
In the ear-consciousness element …pe… in the nose-consciousness element …pe… in the tongue-consciousness element …pe…
Immediately after body-consciousness has arisen and ceased, there arises mind, intellect, mentation, heart,
the clear [mind], the mind-base, the mind-faculty, consciousness, the aggregate of consciousness, the corresponding mind-element,
or else the first act of attention toward all phenomena; [there arises] mind, intellect, mentation, heart, the clear [mind], the mind-base.
The mind-faculty, consciousness, the aggregate of consciousness, and the corresponding mind-element—
this is called the "mind-element.
In this context, what is the "dhamma-element"?

The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, that form which is non-demonstrable and non-reactive and included within the sphere of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana), and the unconditioned element.
Therein, what is the aggregate of feeling?
The aggregate of feeling is of one kind—
Associated with contact.
The aggregate of feeling is twofold:
there is that which is with root-cause, and there is that which is without root-cause.
The aggregate of feeling is threefold:
there is the wholesome, there is the unwholesome, and there is the indeterminate … [and so on] … thus the aggregate of feeling is tenfold … [and so on].
Thus is the aggregate of feeling in its many forms.
This is called the "aggregate of feeling.
In this context, what is the aggregate of perception?
The aggregate of perception is of one kind:
associated with contact.
The aggregate of perception is of two kinds:
There is that which is with cause; there is that which is without cause.
The aggregate of perception is threefold:
there is the wholesome, there is the unwholesome, and there is the indeterminate …pe….
Thus is the aggregate of perception by way of tenfold division...
[and so on] ...thus is the aggregate of perception by way of manifold division.
This is called the "aggregate of perception."
In this context, what is the aggregate of volitional formations?
The aggregate of volitional formations is of one kind:
that which is associated with consciousness.
The aggregate of mental formations is twofold:
there is that which has a cause, and there is that which is without a cause.
The aggregate of mental formations is threefold:
There is the wholesome, there is the unwholesome, there is the indeterminate … [and so on] … thus is the aggregate of volitional formations tenfold;
… [and so on] … thus is the aggregate of volitional formations manifold.
This is called the aggregate of volitional formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).
In that regard, what is form that is non-manifesting, non-reacting, and included within the sphere of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*)?
It is the female faculty ... [and so on] ... up to ... edible food.
This is called form that is "non-demonstrable, non-reactive, and included within the sphere of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana).
In this context, what is the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu)?
It is the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion.
This is called the unconditioned element.
This is called the mental-object element. —17.
In this context, what is the mind-consciousness element?

Immediately after the eye-consciousness element has arisen and ceased, the mind-element arises; immediately after the mind-element has arisen and ceased, consciousness, the mind, the mental faculty … [as above] … the corresponding mind-consciousness element arises.
[The same applies to] the ear-consciousness element … the nose-consciousness element … [and so on].
Immediately after tongue-consciousness-element ... pe ... body-consciousness-element has arisen and ceased, mind-element arises;
immediately after mind-element too has arisen and ceased, consciousness, mind, mentation ... pe ... the corresponding mind-consciousness-element arises.
Dependent on the mind and mental phenomena, consciousness arises— the mind, the mental faculty, the heart, the bright [mind], the mind, the mind-base,
the mind-faculty, consciousness, the aggregate of consciousness, and the corresponding element of mind-consciousness;
this is called the "element of mind-consciousness."
The Exposition by Way of Categories from the Abhidhamma.
3. The Interrogation by Questions.
Eighteen elements:
The eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, the ear-consciousness element;
the nose element, the odor element, the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element;
the body element, the tangible element, the body-consciousness element; the mind element, the mental-object element, the mind-consciousness element.
Of the eighteen elements, how many are wholesome, how many unwholesome, and how many indeterminate? ... [and so on] ... how many are with conflict, and how many are without conflict?
3.1. The Triads:
Sixteen elements are indeterminate.
Two elements may be wholesome, may be unwholesome, or may be indeterminate.
Ten elements should not be described as "associated with pleasant feeling," nor as "associated with painful feeling," nor as "associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."
Five elements are associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The body-consciousness element may be associated with pleasant feeling, or it may be associated with painful feeling.
The mind-consciousness element may be associated with pleasant feeling, it may be associated with painful feeling, or it may be associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The dharma-element may be associated with pleasant feeling, may be associated with painful feeling,

may be associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; or it may not be described as "associated with pleasant feeling," nor as "associated with painful feeling," nor as "associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."
Ten elements are neither resultant nor subject to resultancy.
Five elements are resultants.
The mind element may be a resultant, or it may be neither resultant nor subject to resultancy.
Two elements may be results of kamma, may be subject to becoming results of kamma, or may be neither results of kamma nor subject to becoming results of kamma.
Ten elements are grasped and are objects of clinging.
The sound element is not grasped but is an object of clinging.
Five elements may be both acquired and subject to clinging; they may be neither acquired nor subject to clinging.
Two elements may be both acquired and subject to clinging; they may be neither acquired nor subject to clinging; they may be neither acquired nor subject to clinging.
Sixteen elements are not defiled but are subject to defilement.
Two elements may be both defiled and subject to defilement, may be undefiled but subject to defilement, or may be neither defiled nor subject to defilement.
Fifteen elements are without initial application and without sustained application.
The mind element is with initial application and with sustained application.

The mind-consciousness element may be accompanied by both initial application and sustained application; it may be without initial application and with sustained application only; it may be without both initial application and sustained application.

The mental-object element may be accompanied by both initial application and sustained application; it may be without initial application and with sustained application only; it may be without both initial application and sustained application; or it may not be described as "accompanied by both initial application and sustained application," nor as "without initial application and with sustained application only," nor as "without both initial application and sustained application.
Ten elements are not to be so described.
[The remaining elements] are accompanied by rapture, or accompanied by pleasure, or accompanied by equanimity.
Five elements are accompanied by equanimity.
The body-consciousness element is not accompanied by rapture; it may be accompanied by pleasure, or it may not be accompanied by equanimity, or it may not be said to be "accompanied by pleasure."

Two elements may be accompanied by rapture, may be accompanied by pleasure, or may be accompanied by equanimity; they may also not be described as "accompanied by rapture," "accompanied by pleasure," or "accompanied by equanimity.
Sixteen elements are neither to be abandoned by vision nor by cultivation.
Two elements may be abandoned by vision, may be abandoned by cultivation, or may be neither abandoned by vision nor by cultivation.
Sixteen elements have roots that are neither to be abandoned by vision nor by cultivation.
Two elements may have roots to be abandoned by vision, may have roots to be abandoned by cultivation, or may have roots that are neither to be abandoned by vision nor by cultivation.
Sixteen elements lead neither to accumulation nor to dispersal.
Two elements may be conducive to accumulation, may be conducive to diminution, or may be neither conducive to accumulation nor conducive to diminution.
Sixteen elements are neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Two elements may be learner, may be non-learner, or may be neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Sixteen elements are limited.
Two elements may be limited, may be exalted, or may be immeasurable.
Ten elements are without an object.
Six elements have limited objects.
Two elements may have limited objects, may have exalted objects, may have immeasurable objects, or may not be described as having "limited objects," "exalted objects," or "immeasurable objects.
Sixteen elements are intermediate.
Two elements may be inferior, may be intermediate, or may be superior.
Sixteen elements are indeterminate.
Two elements may be fixed in the wrongness, may be fixed in the rightness, or may be indeterminate.
Ten elements have no object.
Six elements cannot be said to have the Path as their object,
nor to have the Path as their cause, nor to have the Path as their predominance.

Two elements may have the Path as their object, may have the Path as their cause, or may have the Path as their predominance; they may also be such that it cannot be said of them that they "have the Path as their object," "have the Path as their cause," or "have the Path as their predominance.
Ten elements may be arisen, may be bound to arise, or may be such that it cannot be said of them that they are "unarisen.
The sound element may be arisen, may be unarisen, or may be such that it cannot be said of it that it is "bound to arise."
Six elements may be arisen, may be unarisen, or may be subject to arising.
The mental-object element (dhammadhātu) may be arisen, may be unarisen, or may be subject to arising; it should not be said to be "arisen," "unarisen," or "subject to arising.
Seventeen elements may be past, may be future, or may be present.
The dhamma-element may be past, may be future, may be present, or it may not be described as "past," "future," or "present.
Ten elements have no object.
Six elements have a present object.
Two elements may have a past object, may have a future object, may have a present object, or may not be described as having either a past object, a future object, or a present object.
They may be internal, external, or both internal and external.
Ten elements are without objects.
Six elements may have an internal object, may have an external object, or may have both an internal and external object.

Two elements may have an internal object, may have an external object, or may have both an internal and external object; or they may not be described as having an internal object, nor as having an external object, nor as having both an internal and external object.
The visible element is visible and impinging.
Nine elements are non-visible and non-reacting.
Eight elements are non-visible and non-reacting.
3.2. 3.2 Duka (Pairs)
3.2.1. The Group on Causes (Hetugocchaka) Seventeen elements are not causes.
The mental-object element may be a cause, or it may not be a cause.
Sixteen elements are rootless.
Two elements may be with root, or they may be rootless.
Sixteen elements are dissociated from roots.
Two elements may be associated with roots, or they may be dissociated from roots.
Sixteen elements should not be described as "both roots and accompanied by roots," nor as "accompanied by roots but not roots."

The mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) should not be described as "both a cause and accompanied by a cause"; it may be accompanied by a cause but not itself a cause, or it may not be described as "accompanied by a cause but not itself a cause.

The mental-object element (dhammadhātu) may be both a cause and accompanied by a cause, it may be accompanied by a cause but not itself a cause, or it may not be described either as "both a cause and accompanied by a cause" or as "accompanied by a cause but not itself a cause."
The sixteen elements should not be described as "both roots and associated with roots," nor as "associated with roots but not roots.
The mind-consciousness element should not be described [in either way].

Regarding the phrase “both a cause and associated with a cause”: it may be associated with a cause but not itself a cause; it may be such that it cannot be said to be “both a cause and associated with a cause,” nor can it be said to be “associated with a cause but not itself a cause.

The dhamma-element (dhammadhātu) may be both a cause and associated with a cause; it may be associated with a cause but not itself a cause; and it may be such that it cannot be said to be either “both a cause and associated with a cause” or “associated with a cause but not itself a cause.
The sixteen elements are neither causes nor associated with a cause.
The mind-consciousness element may be neither-root-caused-with-root-cause, or it may be neither-root-caused-without-root-cause.

The mental-object element may be neither-root-caused-with-root-cause, or it may be neither-root-caused-without-root-cause, or it may not be called either "neither-root-caused-with-root-cause" nor "neither-root-caused-without-root-cause.
3.2.2. The Short Intermediate Dyad (Cūḷantaraduka)
Seventeen elements are conditioned.
The mental-object element may be conditioned or may be unconditioned.
Seventeen elements are formed.
The dhamma-element may be conditioned or unconditioned.
The visible element is with visibility.
Seventeen elements are without visibility.
Ten elements are with resistance.
Eight elements are without resistance.
Ten elements are material form.
Seven elements are immaterial.
The mental-object element may be material or immaterial.
Sixteen elements are mundane.
Two elements may be mundane, may be supramundane;
they may be cognizable by someone, or not cognizable by anyone.
3.2.3. The Group on the Taints (Āsava-gocchaka).
Seventeen elements are not taints.
The mental-object element may be a taint, or it may not be a taint.
Sixteen elements are accompanied by taints.
Two elements may be with taints (sāsrava), or they may be without taints (anāsrava).
Sixteen elements are dissociated from taints.
Two elements may be associated with taints, or they may be dissociated from taints.
The sixteen elements should not be described as "both taints and subject to taints"; they are subject to taints but are not themselves taints.
The mind-consciousness element should not be described as...
Regarding the phrase “both an outflow and subject to outflows”: it may be subject to outflows but not an outflow; it may be such that it cannot be said to be “both an outflow and subject to outflows.

The dhamma-element may be both an outflow and subject to outflows; it may be subject to outflows but not an outflow; it may be such that it cannot be said to be either “both an outflow and subject to outflows” or “subject to outflows but not an outflow.
The sixteen elements cannot be so described.
“Both taints (*āsava*) and associated with taints,” or “associated with taints but not themselves taints.

The mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) should not be said to be “both a taint and associated with taints”; it may be associated with taints but not itself a taint, or it may not be said to be “associated with taints but not itself a taint.”

The dhamma-element may be both an *āsava* and associated with an *āsava*; it may be associated with an *āsava* but not itself an *āsava*; and it may be such that it cannot be said to be "both an *āsava* and associated with an *āsava*" or "associated with an *āsava* but not itself an *āsava*.
Sixteen elements are dissociated from *āsavas* yet subject to *āsavas*.

Two elements may be dissociated from *āsavas* yet subject to *āsavas*, they may be dissociated from *āsavas* and free from *āsavas*, or they may be such that they cannot be said to be either "dissociated from *āsavas* yet subject to *āsavas*" or "dissociated from *āsavas* and free from *āsavas*."
3.2.4. The Group on Fetters (Saṃyojanagocchaka) Seventeen elements are not fetters.
The mental-object element may be a fetter, or it may not be a fetter.
Sixteen elements are subject to the fetters.
Two elements may be subject to the fetters and may be not subject to the fetters.
Sixteen elements are dissociated from the fetters.
Two elements may be associated with the fetters, or they may be dissociated from the fetters.
Sixteen elements should not be described as "both fetters and objects of the fetters," but rather as "objects of the fetters but not fetters."

The mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) should not be said to be "both a fetter and an object of fettering"; it may be an object of fettering but not a fetter, or it may not be said to be "an object of fettering but not a fetter.
The mental-object element (dhammadhātu) may be both a fetter and an object of fettering, or it may be an object of fettering but not a fetter.
It may not be said that [the remaining factors] are "both fetters and objects of the fetters," nor that they are "objects of the fetters but not fetters.
The sixteen elements should not be said to be "both fetters and associated with the fetters," nor that they are "associated with the fetters but not fetters."

The mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) should not be described as "both a fetter and associated with a fetter"; it may be associated with a fetter but not itself a fetter, or it may not be described as "associated with a fetter but not itself a fetter.
The mental-object element (dhammadhātu) may be both a fetter and associated with a fetter, or it may be associated with a fetter [but not itself a fetter].
And there are those that are neither fetters nor associated with fetters; they should not be described as "both fetters and associated with fetters," nor as "associated with fetters but not fetters.
Sixteen elements are dissociated from fetters but are subject to fetters.

Two elements may be dissociated from the fetters but subject to the fetters; they may be dissociated from the fetters and not subject to the fetters; or they may not be described as either "dissociated from the fetters but subject to the fetters" or "dissociated from the fetters and not subject to the fetters.
3.2.5. The Group on Ties:
Seventeen elements are not ties.
The dhamma-element may be a tie, or it may not be a tie.
Sixteen elements are objects of the ties.
Two elements may be objects of the ties, or they may not be objects of the ties.
Sixteen elements are dissociated from the ties.
Two elements may be associated with the ties, or they may be dissociated from the ties.
Sixteen elements should not be said [to be either].
Regarding the phrase “both fetters and things that are to be fettered”: there are things that are to be fettered but are not themselves fetters.

The mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) should not be described as “both a fetter and something to be fettered”; it may be something to be fettered but is not itself a fetter, or it may not be described as “something to be fettered but is not itself a fetter.”

The element of mental objects (dhammadhātu) may be both a tie and bound by ties; it may be bound by ties but not itself a tie; or it may be so that it cannot be said to be "both a tie and bound by ties" or "bound by ties but not itself a tie.
Sixteen elements cannot be said to be "both ties and associated with ties," nor can they be said to be "associated with ties but not themselves ties."

The mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) should not be said to be "both a tie and associated with ties"; it may be associated with ties but not itself a tie, or it may not be said to be "associated with ties but not itself a tie.
The mental-object element (dhammadhātu) may be both a tie and associated with ties, or it may be associated with ties but not itself a tie.

The [remaining] sixteen elements are dissociated from the ties (gantha-vippayutta) and are subject to the ties (ganthaniya). They may be described as neither "both ties and associated with ties" nor "associated with ties but not ties."

Two elements may be dissociated from the fetters and subject to the fetters; they may be dissociated from the fetters and not subject to the fetters; they may not be described as either "dissociated from the fetters and subject to the fetters" or "dissociated from the fetters and not subject to the fetters.
3.3.2.6. The Group on Floods, Yokes, and Hindrances:
Seventeen elements are not floods... [and so forth].
There are no yokes...
[and so on] ...no hindrances.
The dharma-element may be a hindrance, or it may not be a hindrance.
Sixteen elements are obstructive.
Two elements may be obstructive or may not be obstructive.
Sixteen elements are dissociated from the obstructions.
Two elements may be associated with the hindrances, and may be dissociated from the hindrances.
Sixteen elements should not be described as "both hindrances and objects of the hindrances," but rather as "objects of the hindrances but not hindrances."

The mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) should not be described as "both an hindrance and something that can be hindered. It may be something that can be hindered but is not itself an hindrance; or it may not be described as "something that can be hindered but is not itself an hindrance.

The mental-object element (dhammadhātu) may be both an hindrance and something that can be hindered; it may be something that can be hindered but is not itself an hindrance; or it may not be described either as "both an hindrance and something that can be hindered" or as "something that can be hindered but is not itself an hindrance."
The sixteen elements should not be described as "both hindrances and associated with hindrances," nor as "associated with hindrances but not hindrances.
The mind-consciousness element should not be described as...

“Both an hindrance and associated with an hindrance”: it may be associated with an hindrance but not itself an hindrance; it may be such that it cannot be said to be “both associated with an hindrance and itself an hindrance.
The dhamma-element (dhammadhātu) may be both an hindrance and associated with an hindrance; it may be associated with an hindrance but not itself an hindrance;
it may be such that it cannot be said to be either “both an hindrance and associated with an hindrance” or “associated with an hindrance but not itself an hindrance.”
And also: "obstructive but not itself an obstruction.
Sixteen elements are dissociated from obstructions and are obstructive.

Two elements may be dissociated from obstructions and obstructive; they may be dissociated from obstructions and non-obstructive; or they may be such that it cannot be said whether they are "dissociated from obstructions and obstructive" or "dissociated from obstructions and non-obstructive."
3.2.9. The Group on Grasping (Parāmāsa-gocchaka).
Seventeen elements are not grasping.
The mental-object element may be grasping, or it may not be grasping.
Sixteen elements are objects of clinging.
Two elements may be objects of clinging, or they may not be objects of clinging.
Sixteen elements are dissociated from the taints of clinging.
The mind-consciousness element may be associated with the perversions, or it may be dissociated from the perversions.

The mental-object element may be associated with the perversions, or it may be dissociated from the perversions, or it may not be described as either "associated with the perversions" or "dissociated from the perversions.
Sixteen elements are not to be so described.
“Both misapprehensions and misapprehended”: this refers to those things that are misapprehended but are not themselves misapprehensions.

The mind-consciousness element should not be described as “both a misapprehension and misapprehended”; it may be misapprehended but not a misapprehension, or it may not be described as “misapprehended but not a misapprehension.”

The dhamma-element may be both an object of clinging (*parāmāsa*) and clung-to (*parāmaṭṭha*); it may be clung-to but not an object of clinging; and it may not be described as either "both an object of clinging and clung-to" or "clung-to but not an object of clinging.
Sixteen elements are dissociated from the objects of clinging but are clung-to.

Two elements may be dissociated from the objects of clinging and clung-to; they may be dissociated from the objects of clinging and not clung-to; and they may not be described as either "dissociated from the objects of clinging and clung-to" or "dissociated from the objects of clinging and not clung-to."
3.2.10. The Greater Pairs (Mahantaraduka) Ten elements are without an object;
seven elements have an object.
The dharma-element may have an object, or it may be without an object.
Seven elements are consciousness;
eleven elements are not consciousness.
Seventeen elements are non-mental factors.
The dhamma-element may be mental factors or it may be non-mental factors.
Ten elements are dissociated from consciousness.
The mental-object element may be associated with consciousness, or it may be dissociated from consciousness.
Seven elements should not be described as either "associated with consciousness" or "dissociated from consciousness."
Ten elements are dissociated from consciousness.

“Associated with consciousness,” or “dissociated from consciousness.

Seventeen elements are not conjoined with, originated by, and concomitant with consciousness.

The element of mental phenomena (dhammadhātu) may be conjoined with, originated by, and concomitant with consciousness; it may also not be conjoined with, originated by, or concomitant with consciousness.
Twelve elements are internal;
six elements are external.
Nine elements are derived.
Eight elements are not derived.
The mental-object element may be derived, or it may not be derived.
Ten elements are acquired.
The sound element is not acquired.
Seven elements may be either acquired or not acquired.
3.2.11. Group on Grasping (Upādānagocchaka) Seventeen elements are not grasping.
The mental-object element may be grasping, or it may not be grasping.
Sixteen elements are subject to clinging.
Two elements may be subject to clinging, or they may not be subject to clinging.
Sixteen elements are dissociated from clinging.
Two elements may be associated with clinging, or they may be dissociated from clinging.
Sixteen elements should not be described as "both clinging and objects of clinging," but rather as "objects of clinging but not clinging."

The mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) should not be described as "both clinging and subject to clinging"; it may be subject to clinging but not itself clinging, or it may not be described as "subject to clinging but not itself clinging.

The mental-object element (dhammadhātu) may be both clinging and subject to clinging; it may be subject to clinging but not itself clinging; or it may not be described either as "both clinging and subject to clinging" or as "subject to clinging but not itself clinging."

3.2.12. The Group on Defilements (Kilesagocchaka).
Seventeen elements are not defilements.

The sixteen elements should not be said to be either "both defilements and associated with defilements" or "associated with defilements but not defilements."

Two elements may be dissociated from the defilements yet subject to defilement; they may be dissociated from the defilements and not subject to defilement; or they may be such that it cannot be said whether they are "dissociated from the defilements yet subject to defilement" or "dissociated from the defilements and not subject to defilement.

Two elements may be form-sphere (arūpāvacara), or they may not be form-sphere.
Sixteen elements are included (pariyāpanna).
Two elements may be included, or they may be unincluded (apariyāpanna).
Sixteen elements are not leading out.
Two elements may be leading out, or they may not be leading out.
Sixteen elements are undetermined.
